transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess the main thing is… flying has started feeling way scarier than I think it should. Even just thinking about getting on a plane, I immediately picture this turbulence from my honeymoon flight, and it’s like my brain goes right back there. I know, logically, that people fly safely every day and planes are supposed to be very safe, but that doesn’t really stop the fear from kicking in. It’s gotten to the point where the idea of flying feels overwhelming, and that’s why I’m here.
Do unwanted memories of that honeymoon flight ever suddenly pop into your mind when you’re not trying to think about it?

Um… I’m not sure I’d describe it exactly that way. Like, it’s not as if I’m just sitting at work or making dinner and suddenly I’m fully back on that flight out of nowhere. I don’t think that happens, at least not that I’ve really noticed.

It’s more that when something about flying comes up—like someone mentions a trip, or I see a plane, or I start thinking about booking travel—then my mind immediately goes to that honeymoon flight and the turbulence. But completely unwanted memories popping in when there’s no connection at all… I don’t know. I can’t really say that’s been a big thing for me.
Do you avoid flying because of this fear?

Yes… I do. I mean, I didn’t at first think of it as “avoiding,” because I kept telling myself I was just being practical or saving money or whatever, but honestly, yes. I’ve been choosing to drive really long distances instead of flying, even when flying would make way more sense. Like I’ll look at the flight options and then immediately start figuring out how many hours it would take to drive, where we could stop, how to make it work around my schedule… even if it’s exhausting.

And I’ve turned down work trainings if they’d require me to fly. I work in education administration, so sometimes there are trainings or conferences that would probably be good for me professionally, but if they’re far enough that flying is expected, I just… find a reason not to go. I’ll say the timing doesn’t work or that I can do a different one later.

Even talking about a trip can be hard. If it’s something I absolutely have to discuss, like plans that involve possible flying, I usually need my husband sitting with me. Not even necessarily saying anything the whole time, just being there so I don’t panic and back out immediately. So, yes, I guess I’ve been arranging things around not flying more than I want to admit.
Do you ever have panic attacks that come on out of the blue, when you are not thinking about flying?

I don’t think so… not out of the blue like that. When I feel panicky, it’s usually tied to flying somehow—like I’m looking at tickets, or someone brings up a trip, or I start imagining being on the plane. I can get really worked up in those situations, but I wouldn’t say I’m just sitting there doing something totally unrelated and suddenly having a panic attack for no reason.

I mean, I get stressed like anyone does, but that feels different. The intense fear feeling seems connected to the flying stuff.
During that honeymoon flight, did you believe that you or other people on the plane might die or be seriously injured?

I… I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I remember being really scared, like my body reacted as if something was seriously wrong, but I don’t know that I had a clear thought like, “We’re all going to die,” or “Someone is definitely going to get hurt.”

It was more confused than that, I think. The turbulence felt awful and I hated not knowing what was happening, and I was watching other people and the flight attendants, trying to figure out if I should be more scared. But whether I actually believed we were in real danger of dying or being seriously injured… I don’t know. I can’t honestly say that was a definite thought I had.
Outside of anything related to flying, do you worry excessively about a lot of other parts of your life?

Um… I don’t think so. Not in that “everything is a worry all the time” kind of way, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I worry about normal things—work stuff, whether I’m staying on top of things, family plans, money here and there—but it doesn’t feel excessive or like it takes over my whole life. It’s not like I’m constantly cycling through a bunch of different fears or expecting something bad to happen in every area. Most of the really intense worry, the kind that feels hard to control, seems to come up around flying or even having to think about flying.

So… outside of that, I don’t think I’d describe myself as someone who worries excessively about lots of things.
When you think about flying, is the main thing you fear that the plane will be unsafe?

I think… yes and no. The unsafe part is definitely in there, but it’s not always like a clear, logical thought of, “This plane is unsafe.” It’s more that flying has started to feel way scarier than it probably should. Even just thinking about getting on a plane makes my mind jump back to that honeymoon flight, the turbulence and that feeling of being trapped in it and not knowing what was happening.

And I know, intellectually, people fly safely every day. I know that. I can tell myself that, and I do. But when I’m actually imagining being on the plane, it doesn’t feel reassuring enough. My brain kind of pictures something going wrong anyway, or just remembers how frightening that turbulence felt, and then the whole idea of flying feels unsafe, even if part of me knows that’s not really rational.
Do you try to avoid reminders of that honeymoon flight, like conversations, news, movies, or images about plane turbulence?

Yeah… I think I do, maybe not every single kind of reminder, but definitely the ones that make it feel like I might have to deal with flying again.

Like, I’ll go out of my way to avoid flying now. I’ve chosen really long drives instead of just taking a short flight, even when it made the trip more exhausting and honestly kind of inconvenient for everyone. And with work, there have been trainings or things I probably should have gone to, but if flying was involved, I’d find a reason not to go or just turn it down. I kind of tell myself it’s not worth the hassle, but I know the real reason is that I don’t want to get on a plane.

With conversations, if it’s just someone casually talking about travel, I can sometimes sit through it, but if it turns into talking about a trip I might need to take, I get really tense. I don’t like handling those conversations by myself. If I absolutely have to talk through plans or decide about a trip, I need my husband sitting with me, because otherwise I feel like I’ll just shut it down and back out. He sort of keeps me grounded enough to get through the conversation.
Have you had nightmares about that honeymoon flight?

Um… not really, no. At least not that I can clearly point to and say, “That was a nightmare about the honeymoon flight.”

I mean, I’ve had bad dreams before like anyone does, and sometimes if I’ve been stressed I’ll wake up feeling unsettled, but I don’t remember having recurring nightmares where I’m back on that plane or reliving the turbulence in my sleep. The fear is much more something that comes up when I’m awake and thinking about flying, or when the subject comes up.

So… no, I don’t think nightmares are really a big part of it for me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a marked, cued fear focused specifically on flying, recognizes the fear as excessive relative to actual danger, consistently avoids air travel and related situations, and has occupational and practical impairment. Panic-like symptoms occur only in relation to the phobic trigger. PTSD is not supported because there is no clearly established qualifying traumatic event involving actual/threatened death or serious injury, and no clear intrusive recollections, nightmares, or uncued re-experiencing. Panic disorder and generalized anxiety are also not supported by the interview.
